title: Matching numerals 1 to 5 to groups
keyIdea: A numeral is the written sign for a number, like 3. It tells you how many. To match a numeral to a group, count the things one at a time. The last number you say is how many. Spread out or bunched up, big or small, each thing counts as one. So the numeral 3 goes with any group of three things.

kid: This is the numeral 3. It says three. Can you find three apples? Touch each one and count: one, two, three.
Now find the card for this group. Count the balls. You say 1, 2, 3, 4. The last number is 4. So the card is 4.
Spread the apples far apart. Count again. Still 4! Push them close. Still 4! Moving them does not change how many.
Big balls and tiny beads both count. Two big balls go with the 2 card. Look for numerals on doors, buses and cakes too.
adult: This is early number work on numerals and cardinality. Development Matters asks three and four year olds to link numerals and amounts, for example showing the right number of objects to match the numeral, up to 5. US Common Core K.CC.A.3 asks children to represent a number of objects with a written numeral, and K.CC.B.4 says the last number name said tells the number of objects counted.

Matching rests on three counting principles. One-to-one correspondence means one number word for each object. The stable order means the words always come in the same order. Cardinality means the last word said is the size of the group. Small groups of up to about 4 can also be seen at a glance, which is called subitising.

Common mistakes: thinking a spread-out group has more than a bunched one, which is a failure of conservation of number; picking a bigger numeral for big objects; answering with the first number counted instead of the last; and counting an item twice or skipping one. Children also mix up how numerals look, such as 2 and 5. Be careful not to count for your child. Ask them to touch each item.

In the lab your child puts apples on a plate to match a numeral card, drags numeral cards onto groups that are spread out, bunched up, big or small, finds the group with the wrong card, and matches numerals on a door, a bus and a birthday card.

familyTip: Go on a numeral hunt: house doors, bus fronts, lift buttons and birthday cards. Each time, ask your child to read the numeral and then show you that many fingers, steps or claps.

visual.caption: Which numeral goes with each group? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match plates and cards to numerals, spread out or bunched, big or small, fix a wrong card, and read numerals around you.

practice.prompt: Which group of apples matches the numeral card 4?
practice.hint: Touch each apple and count. Stop when you say the number on the card.
practice.explain: The numeral 4 means four. The group with four apples matches: 1, 2, 3, 4.

practice.prompt: The card shows the numeral {n}. How many blocks do you put next to it?
practice.hint: The numeral tells you how many. Count out one block at a time.
practice.explain: The numeral {n} means {n} blocks. Count them out one at a time and stop at {n}.

practice.prompt: 3 cars are spread far apart. Which numeral card goes with them?
practice.hint: Moving things apart does not add any. Count the cars.
practice.explain: There are 3 cars. Far apart or close together, it is still 3, so the card is 3.

practice.prompt: The plate has {k} apples. The card says 5. How many more apples do you need?
practice.hint: Count on from {k} until you get to 5.
practice.explain: From {k}, count on to 5. That is {=5-k} more apples, then the plate matches the card.

pool.prompt: 2 big balls and 5 small beads. Which numeral goes with the big balls?
pool.hint: Big things still count as one each. Count the balls.
pool.explain: There are two balls, so the numeral is 2. Being big does not make more.

pool.prompt: Sam counts his toy cars: 1, 2, 3. Which card does he pick?
pool.hint: The last number you say tells you how many.
pool.explain: Sam said 3 last, so there are 3 cars and he picks the card 3.

pool.prompt: The door has the numeral {n} on it. Knock that many times. How many knocks is that?
pool.hint: Read the numeral on the door. It tells you how many knocks.
pool.explain: The numeral {n} means {n}, so you knock {n} times.

pool.prompt: Mia has the card 2. She puts out 4 spoons. What is wrong?
pool.hint: Count the spoons. Is it the same as the card?
pool.explain: The card says 2 but there are 4 spoons, so there are too many. She takes 2 away.

pool.prompt: Which numeral is the number five?
pool.hint: Five has a flat top line and a round tummy at the bottom.
pool.explain: 5 is the numeral for five. 2 and 5 can look alike, so check the flat line at the top.

pool.prompt: The cake has {n} candles. Which numeral goes on the birthday card?
pool.hint: Touch each candle and count. The last number is the numeral.
pool.explain: There are {n} candles, so the card shows the numeral {n}.

pool.prompt: 4 apples in a pile and 4 apples in a long line. Which group has more?
pool.hint: Count each group. Does moving the apples change the number?
pool.explain: Both groups have 4 apples, so they are the same. A long line just takes more room.

pool.prompt: The group has 3 bears. The card says 4. What do you do?
pool.hint: Count the bears first. The card must say that many.
pool.explain: There are 3 bears, so the card should be the numeral 3. Close is not a match.
